cover.artAlt: A bright green seedling sprouting from dark soil in morning sunlight, with tiny dew drops on its first leaves
cover.blurb: A tiny green sprout is pushing up through the soil, still sparkling with drops of morning dew. Turn the page to discover how one little seed becomes a towering plant.

pages.title: A Seed Wakes Up
pages.artAlt: A close-up of a seed splitting open with a tiny white root poking into dark soil

facts.text: Before a seed can grow, it needs a big drink of water. As the seed soaks the water up, its coat swells and softens until it splits open and wakes up. Scientists call this first long drink imbibition.

The very first part of a plant to push out of a seed is a tiny root. It reaches down into the soil to hold the seed in place and start drinking up water. Gardeners call this little first root the radicle.
facts.artAlt: A close-up of a bean seed with its coat split open and one small white root pushing out into dark soil
facts.caption: The very first root pushes out of a seed that has split open.

facts.text: That first root always seems to know which way is down. Special cells in its tip can sense gravity, so the root grows downward into the soil while the shoot heads up toward the light. This clever sense of direction is called gravitropism.
facts.artAlt: A cut-away view of soil showing a sprouted seed with its white root curving downward and a pale shoot heading up
facts.caption: The root heads down, the shoot heads up.

infographic.title: The first three things a seed does

stops.label: It takes a long drink of water until its coat splits open
A tiny first root called the radicle pushes out
The root senses which way is down and heads into the soil

infographic.caption: Scientists call that first long drink imbibition, and the root's sense of which way is down gravitropism.

pages.title: Reaching for the Sun
pages.artAlt: A young seedling with two little leaves growing in a sunny garden bed

facts.text: The first two little leaves on a seedling are not quite like the leaves that come later. They are called seed leaves, or cotyledons, and they were tucked inside the seed the whole time. They carry a packed lunch of food and can turn green to help feed the young plant.

Once the leaves open in the sunshine, they get to work like tiny food factories. They catch sunlight and mix it with water and gas from the air to make a sugar the plant can eat. As they do this they give off oxygen, which is part of the air we breathe.
facts.artAlt: A young seedling in a sunny garden bed with the sunlight glowing through its two open leaves
facts.caption: Sunlight glows right through a seedling's first leaves.

facts.text: Have you noticed how a seedling on a windowsill leans toward the glass? Young plants can bend and grow toward the light so their leaves catch as much sunshine as possible. This gentle stretch toward the sun is called phototropism.
facts.artAlt: A potted seedling on a bright windowsill leaning noticeably toward the glass
facts.caption: A seedling on a windowsill leans toward the light.

infographic.title: A leaf is a little food factory
infographic.name: leaf-factory
infographic.caption: Leaves catch sunlight and mix it with water and a gas from the air to make a sugar the plant can eat. The oxygen they give off is part of the air we breathe.

pages.title: Busy Roots Underground
pages.artAlt: A close-up of delicate white roots spreading through dark soil inside a glass container

facts.text: If you look very closely at a root, you might spot fuzzy little threads called root hairs. These tiny, hair-like parts are the main place where a plant drinks up water and takes in the minerals it needs from the soil.
Roots do much more than drink. They spread out through the soil to anchor the plant and support it, holding it steady so wind and rain cannot easily knock it over.
facts.artAlt: A plant lifted out of the ground with its full root ball intact, pale roots spreading through dark soil
facts.caption: A whole root ball, holding the plant steady.

facts.text: Those pale little root hairs are very delicate and can be damaged easily. That is why a plant may droop for a while after it is moved, because some of its tiny root hairs get broken as it settles into a new home.
facts.artAlt: A close-up of the very fine white root hairs along a young plant root
facts.caption: The fine root hairs that do the drinking, close up.

infographic.title: Where a plant actually drinks
infographic.name: root-hairs
infographic.caption: Root hairs are so small you would need a magnifying glass to see them, and they are the main place a plant takes in water and minerals. They break easily, which is why a plant droops for a while after it is moved.

pages.title: Sunflowers and the Sun
pages.artAlt: A wide field of tall sunflowers in full bloom all facing the same direction

facts.text: While a sunflower is still young and growing, it follows the sun across the sky each day. The east side of its stem grows a little more in the daytime to swing the flower to face west by evening, then it slowly turns back again overnight.

Here is a surprise. Once a sunflower is fully grown and blooming, it stops following the sun and settles down facing east. So a whole field of open sunflowers greets the sunrise together every morning.
facts.artAlt: A wide field of open sunflowers at sunrise with every bloom facing the low morning sun
facts.caption: A whole field of open sunflowers greets the sunrise together.

facts.text: Facing east turns out to be a clever trick. The morning sun warms these blooms up quickly, and warm flowers are inviting to bees. Sunflowers that face east attract about five times as many pollinating insects as ones facing the other way.
facts.artAlt: A honeybee on the golden center of a sunflower in warm morning light
facts.caption: Warm morning flowers are inviting to bees.

infographic.title: Which way do the bees go?
infographic.caption: Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley found that east-facing sunflowers attract about five times as many pollinating insects, because the morning sun warms those blooms up first.
